title: Oscar Romero (1917–1980)
hookLine: an archbishop in El Salvador, shot while celebrating Mass, now honored as a saint

lines: A SERMON THAT READS THE NEWS.
cards: Sunday morning in El Salvador, and in kitchens and market stalls, radios are tuned to the archdiocese's station. The archbishop is preaching from the cathedral, and he goes on a long time. He explains the readings.
Then he does something sermons don't usually do: he reads the news of the week. The names of people killed. People taken from their homes and not seen again.
A village where soldiers came. He reads them out so that they will be heard by someone. The man at the microphone was Óscar Romero.

teach.b: Romero's story turns four times. First, the quiet bishop. When he was made archbishop of San Salvador he was known as a careful, bookish priest, and some expected him to keep his head down.

teach.h: A FRIEND KILLED ON A COUNTRY ROAD.
teach.b: Soon after, his friend Rutilio Grande, a Jesuit priest who worked among poor farmers, was shot dead on a country road along with companions. Romero went to see the bodies and prayed over them that night.
People who knew him say something changed in him there. Third, the voice.

teach.h: THE RADIO HOMILIES NAME THE DEAD.
teach.b: From then on his homilies, carried by radio, named what was happening to his people, and he said the Church had to be the voice of those who had no voice.
A line in Proverbs sounds like his work, in the Douay-Rheims: "Open thy mouth for the dumb." Dumb there means those who cannot speak. In his last Sunday homily he turned to the soldiers themselves.
They were farmers' sons too, he reminded them, killing their own brothers and sisters, and he asked them, in God's name, to stop. Fourth, the altar.

teach.h: SHOT AT THE ALTAR, NOW A SAINT.
teach.b: The next day, as he finished his homily at Mass in the chapel of the hospital where he lived, a gunman shot him at the altar.

teach.h: OPEN THY MOUTH FOR THE DUMB.
teach.b: The Church has since declared him a martyr and a saint, canonized alongside Paul the Sixth. He never ran for anything or carried a weapon. He read the Gospel on Sunday, and then he read out the names.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Óscar Romero, and in El Salvador and elsewhere people gather where he died, at the hospital chapel in San Salvador, and at his tomb in the cathedral.

games.q: you're Romero, a cautious new archbishop. your friend has been killed for standing with poor farmers. what do you do?
o: keep quiet; your job is to keep the peace.
speak, and keep speaking, for those who have no voice.
leave the country for a safer post.
games.why: he stayed and preached, naming the dead on the Sunday radio, until he too was killed.

practice: Let someone come to mind whose story doesn't get told: a worker at the edge of your town, a neighbor who doesn't speak the language, someone in a place the news has forgotten.
Say their situation to yourself in one plain sentence, the way Romero read the names. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
